questions.stem: The human heart is a four-chambered organ. Which two chambers pump blood to the lungs and the rest of the body respectively?

options.option_text: Left atrium (to lungs) and right ventricle (to body)
Right ventricle (to lungs) and left ventricle (to body)
Right atrium (to lungs) and left atrium (to body)
Both ventricles pump to lungs; atria pump to body

questions.explanation: The RIGHT VENTRICLE pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs via the pulmonary artery (pulmonary circulation). The LEFT VENTRICLE pumps oxygenated blood to the body via the aorta (systemic circulation). Atria receive blood — left atrium from lungs (pulmonary veins), right atrium from body (vena cavae) — but atria don't pump to the aorta or pulmonary artery; that's the ventricles' job.

questions.stem: Which blood group is called the 'universal donor'?
questions.explanation: O negative (O−) blood has NO A, B, or Rh antigens — so it can be transfused to any recipient without triggering an immune reaction. It is thus the UNIVERSAL DONOR. AB+ is the UNIVERSAL RECIPIENT (has all antigens, no anti-A/anti-B antibodies). O+ can donate to all Rh+ recipients but not Rh−, making it a partial donor. In true emergencies, O− is preferred when the recipient's blood type is unknown.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of blood plasma?
questions.explanation: Blood plasma is the LIQUID portion of blood, containing water (~90%), proteins (albumin, globulin, fibrinogen), electrolytes, hormones, nutrients, and waste products. Erythrocytes (RBCs), leukocytes (WBCs), and thrombocytes (platelets) are the CELLULAR components — they are SUSPENDED in plasma but not part of it. Plasma constitutes ~55% of blood volume; the cells are the other ~45%.

questions.stem: What is the normal range of a healthy adult's resting heart rate?
questions.explanation: The normal RESTING heart rate for a healthy adult is 60–100 BPM (beats per minute). Below 60 = bradycardia (sometimes normal in athletes). Above 100 = tachycardia. Newborns have much higher rates (120–160 BPM); children's rates decrease with age. Elite endurance athletes can have resting rates as low as 40 BPM without being pathological.

questions.stem: Which of the following carries oxygen in the red blood cells?
questions.explanation: HEMOGLOBIN is the iron-containing protein in RBCs that binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues. Each Hb molecule has 4 subunits (2α + 2β chains), each with a haem group containing Fe²⁺. Myoglobin is the oxygen-storage protein in MUSCLE tissue (not RBCs). Cytochrome is a mitochondrial electron-transport protein. Chlorophyll is the PLANT photosynthetic pigment (Mg²⁺-based, not Fe-based).

questions.explanation: The SA (sinoatrial) node, located in the RIGHT ATRIUM, initiates each heartbeat by generating electrical impulses at ~60–100 per minute. It's called the natural pacemaker. The AV node receives the SA impulse, delays it slightly (to allow atrial contraction), and then passes it to the Bundle of His, which divides into Purkinje fibres that trigger ventricular contraction. Artificial cardiac pacemakers REPLACE the SA node when it fails. sinoatrial node.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is caused by an abnormality of hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Sickle-cell anaemia is a genetic disorder caused by a single-point mutation in the HBB gene (Glu → Val at position 6 of β-chain), producing abnormal HbS. Under low oxygen, HbS polymerises, distorting RBCs into sickle shapes — blocking capillaries and causing crises. Diabetes = insulin/pancreas issue. Scurvy = Vitamin C deficiency. Rickets = Vitamin D deficiency. Thalassemia is another Hb disorder (reduced α/β-chain synthesis).

questions.stem: William Harvey, in 1628, published findings that established which of the following?

options.option_text: Humans have 4 blood groups (A, B, AB, O)
Blood circulates in a closed loop through the body, pumped by the heart
Red blood cells carry oxygen via hemoglobin

questions.explanation: William Harvey's 1628 book 'De Motu Cordis' (On the Motion of the Heart) established the THEORY OF CIRCULATION — that blood circulates in a closed loop pumped by the heart, rather than being continuously produced by the liver (as Galen had taught for 1400 years). ABO blood groups were discovered by Karl Landsteiner (1901). Hemoglobin's role in O2 transport was identified by Felix Hoppe-Seyler (1864). Platelets in clotting were characterized in the 19th–20th c.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the function of valves in the human heart?

options.option_text: Valves prevent backflow of blood between heart chambers and into the ventricles from the pulmonary artery/aorta

questions.explanation: The heart has four valves that prevent backflow: TRICUSPID (between right atrium & right ventricle), PULMONARY (right ventricle → pulmonary artery), MITRAL/BICUSPID (left atrium & left ventricle), AORTIC (left ventricle → aorta). The 'lub-dub' heart sound is produced by valve closure (lub = AV valves closing, dub = semilunar valves closing). Faulty valves cause murmurs or regurgitation.

questions.stem: What is the average lifespan of a human red blood cell?
questions.explanation: Mature erythrocytes (RBCs) circulate for approximately 120 days (about 4 months) before being broken down by macrophages in the spleen and liver. During this time they travel ~400 km in the bloodstream. New RBCs are produced in the RED BONE MARROW at ~2 million per second. Platelets live ~7–10 days (distractor A); WBC lifespan varies from hours (neutrophils) to years (memory lymphocytes).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of blood?

options.option_text: Transport of oxygen, nutrients, and hormones
Maintenance of body temperature via heat distribution
Immune defence via white blood cells and antibodies
Digestion of proteins into amino acids

questions.explanation: Blood transports (O₂, CO₂, nutrients, hormones, waste), regulates (pH, temperature, fluid balance), and protects (immune response, clotting). Protein DIGESTION happens in the STOMACH (HCl + pepsin) and small intestine (trypsin, chymotrypsin, peptidases) — secreted by pancreas and gastric cells. Absorbed amino acids then enter blood via portal circulation, but the digestion itself is NOT a blood function.
